title: Functions, scope and swapping
overview: Module 17 splits programs into functions. It covers the four basic shapes (with or without parameters, with or without a return value), and then scope: which variables a function can see. The swap examples show why passing a plain value can't change the caller's variable, and how global variables or pointers work around that.

concepts.explain: A `void` function returns nothing, and an `int` function hands back a value with `return`. Parameters are inputs passed in brackets. Any combination of the two is allowed.
concepts.snippet:
void greet();
int add(int a, int b);

concepts.explain: Code in `main` runs line by line. A call jumps into the function, runs all of it, and comes back to the next step in `main`.
`return sum;` sends a value back. The caller can store it (`int r = add();`) or use it directly inside `printf`.
Variables declared inside a function belong only to that function. Two functions can each have their own `a`, at different addresses.
Variables declared outside every function can be seen by all functions declared after them. They start at 0.
C copies each argument into the parameter. Changing the parameter never changes the caller's variable.
To change the caller's variable, pass `&a` and change `*x` inside the function.
concepts.snippet:
void swap(int *x, int *y){ int t=*x; *x=*y; *y=t; }
swap(&a, &b);

files.title: void functions with no parameters
files.what: `greetings()` only prints. `add()` reads two numbers, adds them and prints the sum. Neither function takes parameters or returns a value.
steps: `main` calls `greetings()`, which prints `Hello`.
`main` then calls `add()`, which prints a prompt and reads `a` and `b`.
`add` prints `Function called` and `Sum: a+b`.
Control goes back to `main`, which returns 0.
files.output_note: `Hello`, then `Enter two numbers: Function called` on one line (the prompt has no newline, and typed input doesn't show when it comes from a file), then `Sum: 15`.

check.q: Can `main` use the sum that `add()` computed?
check.a: No. It is a local variable, and the function returns nothing.

files.title: void functions with parameters
files.what: `add(a, b)` gets its numbers as parameters and prints their sum. `alphacheck(ch)` reports whether a letter is lowercase or uppercase.
steps: `main` reads `a` and `b`, then calls `add(a, b)`, which prints `function called` and the sum.
`alphacheck('a')` checks `'a' <= ch && ch <= 'z'`, which is true, so it prints `Lowercase`.
`alphacheck('B')` fails that check and prints `Uppercase`.
files.watch_out: `alphacheck` calls anything that isn't `a`–`z` uppercase, even a digit like `'5'`. Check `'A'..'Z'` explicitly if that matters.

check.q: Why is this `add` more reusable than the one in the previous file?
check.a: It works on any values the caller passes in, instead of always reading them from input.

files.title: Function that returns a value
files.what: `int add()` reads two numbers and returns their sum. `main` calls it twice and stores each result.
steps: `main` prints `Before calling function sum()`.
`result = add()`: the function reads 3 and 4, prints `function called` and returns 7.
`main` prints the after-message and `Result: 7`.
The second call reads 10 and 25 and returns 35, which is stored in `result2`.
files.input_note: One pair of numbers for each call.
files.output_note: Two blocks of output: `function called` / `After calling…` / `Result: 7`, and then the same with `Result: 35`. The messages show the order in which things run.

check.q: What does `return` do besides giving back the value?

files.title: Using global variables
files.what: `a` and `b` are global, so `add()` can read them without any parameters. `main` sets them, calls `add`, changes them and calls `add` again.
steps: `int a, b;` is declared above every function.
`main` sets `a = 10` and `b = 20`, then prints `add()`, which gives 30.
`main` sets `a = 30` and `b = 40`, and `add()` now gives 70.
`Function called` shows up just before each `Sum is` line, because `add()` runs while `printf` is collecting its arguments.
files.output_note: `Before…`, `After…`, `Function called`, `Sum is 30`, `After…`, `Function called`, `Sum is 70`. The "After calling" text is printed before the call actually happens.
files.watch_out: Globals make it hard to see which function changes what. Prefer parameters.

check.q: What does `add()` return if `main` never sets `a` and `b`?

files.title: Why a naive swap fails
files.what: `swap()` declares its own local `a` and `b` and swaps them. `main`'s variables are separate and don't change.
steps: `main` has `a = 10` and `b = 20` and prints their addresses.
`swap()` declares new `a` and `b` at different addresses, then swaps them to 20 and 10.
Back in `main`, the original `a` and `b` are still 10 and 20.
files.output_note: The addresses printed inside `main` and inside `swap` are different, which proves they are different variables. `Inside function` shows `a = 20, b = 10`, but `After calling` still shows `a = 10, b = 20`.
files.watch_out: `swap(a, b)` passes arguments to a function declared as `swap()`. Older C accepts this and ignores them, but C23 compilers reject it. Even `void swap(int a, int b)` would fail to swap, because the parameters are only copies.

check.q: Would `void swap(int a, int b)` fix it?
check.a: No. The parameters are copies, so only the copies would be swapped.

files.title: Swapping global variables
files.what: With global `a` and `b`, `main` and `swap()` use the very same variables, so a swap inside `swap()` does reach `main`.
steps: `int a, b;` is global, so both start at 0.
`main` and `swap` print the same pair of addresses.
`swap()` exchanges `a` and `b` using `temp`.
`main` prints the values again.
files.output_note: The addresses match in both functions. But the values are `a = 0, b = 0` before and after, because swapping two zeros changes nothing you can see.
files.watch_out: **The demo doesn't show a swap:** `a` and `b` are never given values. Add `a = 10; b = 20;` at the start of `main` to see `a = 20, b = 10`. `swap(a, b)` also passes arguments to a function with no parameters, which C23 compilers reject. Call `swap()` instead.

check.q: Why do the addresses match here but not in `scope_swap_not_working.c`?
check.a: Here both functions use the same global variables. There, each function had its own local ones.

files.title: Swap that works: pass addresses
files.what: `swap(&a, &b)` gives the function the addresses, so writing to `*x` and `*y` changes `main`'s variables.
steps: `main` has `a = 10` and `b = 20` and prints their addresses.
`swap(&a, &b)` passes the two addresses into `x` and `y`.
Inside `swap`, `&x` and `&y` are the addresses of the pointer variables themselves, so they differ from `main`'s.
`temp = *x; *x = *y; *y = temp;` changes the values stored at `main`'s addresses.
files.output_note: The final line is `a = 20, b = 10`, so the swap worked. The addresses printed inside `swap` are those of `x` and `y`, not of `a` and `b`.
files.watch_out: To compare with `main`'s addresses, print `x` and `y`, not `&x` and `&y`.

recap: Functions come in four shapes: with or without parameters, and with or without a return value.
A call runs the whole function and then comes back to the caller.
Local variables belong only to their function. Globals are shared and start at 0.
C copies arguments, so changing a parameter never changes the caller's variable.
Pass addresses (`&a`) and use `*` to change the caller's data.

check_yourself.q: What does `void` mean as a return type?
check_yourself.a: The function doesn't return a value.

check_yourself.q: Why can two functions both declare a variable named `a` without a clash?
check_yourself.a: Each local `a` belongs only to its own function and has its own memory.

check_yourself.q: Name two ways to let a function change `main`'s variables.
check_yourself.a: Make the variables global, or pass their addresses as pointers. Pointers are usually the better choice.
